## 1. Narrative Arc

Across six quarters the Chewy story has moved in one consistent direction: from "can this company grow customers again?" to "how fast can margins compound while customers grow steadily?" That is an unusually clean, un-contradicted arc for a maturing e-commerce platform.

At the start of the window (the fiscal Q4 2024 call in March 2025), the headline anxiety was customer count. Chewy had just posted "our first year-over-year growth in eight quarters" in active customers (20.5 million) and management leaned hard on the phrase "we believe we have reached an inflection point." The growth drivers emphasized then — Autoship loyalty (the program where customers set recurring auto-replenishment orders), sponsored ads, and vet clinics — are the same drivers emphasized now, which is a good sign: the story has been added to, not swapped out.

What got introduced and then scaled over the window: (1) Chewy Plus, the paid membership program, went from "out of beta" (Q1) to "roughly 3% of monthly sales" (Q2) to "80% of member mix now paid" with a price increase from $49 to $79 (Q3) — a textbook ramp. (2) Chewy Vet Care clinics grew from 8 locations to 18 across the year. (3) A fresh-food private brand ("Get Real," August 2025) and a unified owned-brand platform ("Chewy Made," 2026). (4) By the final call, an AI-cost-efficiency story was layered on top — "low tens of millions" of savings in 2026, "approximately $50 million or more in annualized savings" by 2027.

Nothing material was quietly dropped. The one quiet de-emphasis: the early hope (Q4 2024) that the post-pandemic e-commerce migration might re-accelerate. By the final call management explicitly stopped underwriting any rebound — "we are not underwriting a meaningful rebound" in pet household formation, and "our model does not depend on a minimum net sales growth threshold to expand profitability." That is a maturity admission, framed (fairly) as a strength: margin expansion is now self-driven, not demand-dependent.

The cleanest divergence: management talks in adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow, where the trajectory is excellent; the screener's GAAP quality scores (Piotroski 4 of 9, ROIC 3.9%, net margin 1.8%) look mediocre because heavy share-based compensation depresses reported profit. **Rising and remarkably steady** — one of the more consistent management voices in the consumer-cyclical universe.

- Q1 2025: "the momentum at Chewy continues… growing confidence in our ability to deliver on the long-term financial model."
- Q2/Q3 2025: increasingly offensive — "profits once again growing faster than sales," "structural resilience of our model."
- Q4 2025 (Mar 2026): the most assertive of all — leading not with results but with a strategic-vision essay, and stating the model "does not depend on a minimum net sales growth threshold to expand profitability."

The language shifted from defensive to offensive over the window — the healthy direction. Guidance got *more* specific (quantified net-add ranges of 150,000–250,000 per quarter; quantified AI savings), not less.

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**High.** The screener shows a beat rate of 5 of 7 quarters (71%), and the transcripts corroborate it: "exceeded the high end of our guidance range" recurs for net sales in fiscal Q1, Q2, and Q3 2025. Management raised full-year net-sales guidance by $175M mid-year (Q2) and delivered. The Q1 fiscal 2026 print (June 2026) again beat, with adjusted EBITDA margin of 7.5% well ahead of the prior-year 6.2%.

There is a mild, benign sandbagging pattern — management repeatedly frames the industry as "stable, not accelerating" and refuses to underwrite a rebound, setting a low external bar it then clears. Reliability: **High.**

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

Analysts pushed hardest on three things; management answered all three with substance rather than deflection:
- **Chewy Plus economics** (Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, William Blair): real if guarded data — incrementality, paid-mix at 80%, gross margins "in line with the enterprise" after the price hike. Not evasive.
- **CVC vet-clinic unit economics**: management repeatedly promised a "detailed review memo" / "look under the hood" — a deferral pending several quarters. This is the one recurring soft non-answer; the clinics are praised qualitatively ("fastest NSPAC compounder") but the return on clinic capital has not been laid out.
- **CFO turnover**: David Reeder left mid-2025 for a semiconductor CEO role; an interim bridged two quarters; Chris Deppe (internal, since 2022) was named permanent by the Q4 2025 call. Cleanly managed.

🟢 Margin trajectory is the rare case of numbers beating the narrative — adjusted EBITDA margin 4.8% → 7.5% in roughly a year.
🟢 Autoship at ~84% of sales (Q1 FY2026) gives subscription-like revenue visibility unusual for a retailer.
🟢 Self-funded buybacks alongside record free cash flow; net-cash balance sheet; capex running *below* the low end of guidance (~1.3% of sales).
🟢 Guidance discipline — explicitly refuses to bank on a category rebound.

🔴 The dominant overhang is the controlling holder, BC Partners. It has been steadily selling — most recently ~$1B / 23.9M shares — and still holds ~88% of the *voting* power via Class B super-voting shares even as its economic stake fell toward ~47%. Public shareholders are minority economic owners with almost no vote, and the recurring secondaries are a structural, mechanical source of selling pressure.
🔴 GAAP returns are thin (ROIC 3.9%, net margin 1.8%) and reported net income fell 43% year over year — accounting earnings lag cash earnings, largely on heavy stock-based compensation.
🔴 Insider open-market activity is one-directional: zero open-market buys against 35 sells (~44M shares) — no insider is stepping in at the lows.
🔴 The vet-clinic return-on-capital "review memo" has been promised and deferred for multiple quarters.

## 7. Hidden Signals

- Terminology migrated from "inflection point" (a one-time turn) to "flywheel" and "layer cake" (a self-reinforcing system) — management now frames growth as structural, not a rebound.
- The new CFO (Deppe) is an internal continuity hire after a brief external CFO; the message is "no strategy change," which the steady guidance supports.
- The most important quiet shift: the pivot to "margin expansion independent of net-sales growth." Management is preparing investors for low-single-digit revenue growth where the equity return comes from margin and free-cash-flow compounding plus buybacks. That is the actual investment case, stated almost in passing.
- Competition is discussed with notable calm — Amazon is named only obliquely; the framed edge is "scaled e-commerce with the service of a local neighborhood pet store," leaning on Autoship habit rather than price.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Margins are compounding ahead of plan, free cash flow is at records, the balance sheet is net cash, and capital is being returned via buyback — all while management refuses to bank on a demand rebound. Execution is genuinely good.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is not a hidden-value or activist setup — it is a quality-compounder-at-a-de-rated-price setup whose chief feature is a *negative* technical, not a positive catalyst. The stock sits near 52-week lows ($17–20 against a $43 high) primarily because the controlling holder, BC Partners, is mechanically selling large blocks while keeping voting control. The director must decide whether accelerating margins and free cash flow can overwhelm a known, recurring overhang from a forced seller who still controls the vote. There is no hard date that ends the overhang and no governance reset on offer — the dual-class structure entrenches BC Partners. The value is real; the re-rating trigger is absent.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and stable-to-widening.** A switching-cost / habit moat (Autoship ~84% of sales) plus a scale-cost edge in fulfillment — real, but not impregnable against Amazon and Walmart, and the thin 3.9% ROIC says the durable base is not yet wide. The trend is favorable (rising margins and Autoship penetration are the signature of a *widening*, not eroding, moat), but it remains narrow in absolute terms.

**Secular force:** Chewy is on the *winning* side of the retail channel-shift (e-commerce taking share from brick-and-mortar pet stores), not a victim. The structural risk to terminal value is competitive (Amazon/Walmart price and logistics), not a one-way secular decline. The cheapness is closer to a fear-and-forced-selling print than a structurally-shrinking base — manageable, not terminal.

In the quarter ended 2 August 2026 the margin was 6.8% against 5.9% a year earlier, and selling and administrative costs fell 70 basis points as a share of sales. Management said on 25 March 2026 that 'our model does not depend on a minimum net sales growth threshold to expand profitability', and for six straight quarters that has been true. On 9 September 2026 the company raised the low end of its full-year margin guidance and raised its sales range, implying about $912 million of adjusted operating cash profit for the year.

The revenue base is unusually hard to dislodge. Autoship - the automatic repeat-delivery subscription - was 84.6% of sales in the latest quarter and grew 9.3%, faster than the company's 7.3%. Active customers reached 21.7 million, up 3.8%, with 208,000 net additions in the quarter and improvement in new customers, reactivations and churn simultaneously. Spend per active customer reached $602, up 3.8% adjusting for the extra week in the prior-year comparison. In a category management itself describes as 'broadly flat year-over-year', Chewy grew organically 5.7% - two to three times the market - and its hard-goods line grew in the mid-teens.

Three high-value businesses are embedded inside a low-multiple retailer. Sponsored advertising - selling ad space on Chewy's own site - carries incremental economics close to a software business and management has a stated ceiling of 3% of enterprise sales against roughly 1.5%-2% today. Chewy Health is now about 30% of revenue and spans pharmacy, compounding (management notes only two credible compounders exist nationally, and the gross margin exceeds pharmacy), insurance, business-to-business software and a clinic network. Chewy Vet Care delivered triple-digit revenue growth in the latest quarter and is described as the fastest compounder of spend per customer in the business. The April 2026 purchase of Modern Animal added 29 owned clinics, round-the-clock virtual care and roughly 100,000 customers, of which 40%-50% are new to Chewy - and those customers are not yet in guidance.

Returns on capital corroborate the story rather than contradicting it: about 12.9% on invested capital on a trailing basis, against 3.3% at Petco and 5.8% at Central Garden & Pet. Gross margin, operating margin and returns are all rising together, which is the signature of a widening moat, not an eroding one. The cash conversion cycle is negative by about three days, so growth funds itself.

Finally, the company is shrinking itself. Diluted shares fell from 428.4 million to 410.1 million over the year, about 4%, on $400.0 million of buybacks in the first half alone - 17.5 million shares retired, with $350.1 million of authorisation left - with the chief financial officer stating on 9 September 2026 that 'we continue to believe that Chewy shares are undervalued at current levels'. Artificial intelligence adds a quantified, self-help profit lever: low tens of millions of dollars of savings this year, scaling to about $50 million annualised next year.

Conditions the bull case depends on: the pet category stays flat rather than contracting; organic growth holds at or above 5%; gross margin declines in the third quarter only by the guided seasonal amount once the one-off benefits reverse; Modern Animal integrates without a margin surprise and the clinic model earns an acceptable return on the capital sunk into it; and the buyback continues to outrun stock compensation so per-share cash flow keeps compounding even if total cash flow only grows modestly.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Chewy is a bad business. It is that the headline cheapness is an accounting illusion and the company has quietly changed shape.

Start with the cash. Reported free cash flow of $568 million over the past twelve months, or roughly $730 million guided for the full year, looks like an 8.6% yield on an $8.5 billion market value. But about $320 million a year of that is share-based compensation - stock handed to employees - added back as a non-cash item. Chewy then spends real cash buying shares to stop the count rising: $400.0 million, or 17.5 million shares, in the first half of this year. Net the two and genuine cash available to owners is roughly $250-400 million, a 3%-5% yield. On reported earnings the picture is plainer still: about $0.78 a share this year and consensus of roughly $1.06 for the year to January 2028, putting the stock at 26 times this year and 19 times next. That is not a distressed multiple. It is a fair one for a company growing revenue 6%.

Growth is decelerating and is increasingly purchased. Organic growth - excluding acquisitions - fell from 8.3% in mid-2025 to 5.7% in the quarter ended 2 August 2026. The 7.3% headline includes SmartPak and Modern Animal, bought for $552.8 million of cash in six months at what appear to be multiples of sales. Spend per active customer grew just 1.9% as reported. Treats - the discretionary slice of consumables - slowed materially faster than core food, and management refused, when asked directly by Guggenheim on the latest call, to size how large treats are. The category has no pricing power at all: management expects 'little or no contribution from pricing' and is not underwriting any recovery in pet household formation.

The latest quarter's profit beat was manufactured by timing. Management disclosed that roughly $10 million of tariff refunds arrived early, rebates shifted forward out of the second half, and over $5 million came from gift-card breakage, inventory adjustments and vendor-funded merchandising - and that these items 'accounted for essentially all of the adjusted EBITDA outperformance'. Gross margin was flat year over year at 30.4% despite those benefits, and management has pre-warned that it will fall sequentially in the third quarter, while advertising spend rises and fuel remains a headwind. In other words, the third quarter is engineered to look worse than the second on every visible line.

The balance sheet identity has changed, even though the leverage has not. In December 2025 the company described itself as debt-free with $1.5 billion of liquidity. On 23 June 2026 it drew an inaugural $600 million seven-year term loan at Term SOFR plus 1.75%, a weighted-average 5.41%, and at 2 August 2026 it carried $591.7 million of debt - $3.0 million current and $588.7 million long-term, net - against $612.2 million of cash and marketable securities. That is net cash of $20.5 million, not net debt: the $527.2 million once counted here as capitalised leases is the non-current operating lease liability, rent is expensed within selling and administrative costs at $30.3 million in the quarter and $57.6 million in the half, so operating cash profit is already struck after it, and the $42.3 million current lease liability does not belong inside borrowings either. So the bear case does not rest on leverage. It rests on where the money went: $552.8 million of cash bought 29 physical veterinary clinics (Modern Animal, $378.0 million, closed 21 May 2026) and an equine supplements business management says 'requires a little bit of fixing' (SmartPak, $174.8 million, closed 2 February 2026). Veterinary roll-ups are capital-hungry, constrained by a national shortage of veterinarians, and have a long industry record of being overpaid for. Management concedes Modern Animal is a drag on margin. Not one analyst question in six earnings calls has interrogated the return on capital of this pivot, and a company with a negative cash conversion cycle took a seven-year secured loan to fund it.

Management's judgement about its own end market has been demonstrably poor exactly once, and recently. On 25 March 2026 the chief executive told investors the category was 'steady and resilient to macro trends' with 'no evidence of deterioration'. By 10 June 2026 guidance had been reset. He later dated the break to 'the late March, April time frame' - five weeks after the reassurance.

The supply picture is one-directional: zero open-market insider purchases against 26 sales totalling roughly 41.2 million shares. And the macro backdrop is hostile to exactly this asset - a hiking Federal Reserve, the ten-year Treasury at its first close above 5% since 2007, oil near $100 and consumer sentiment at 47.8. A 19-times-forward consumer name whose incremental buyer was a growth fund is precisely the duration the market is repricing.

What would confirm the bear case: organic growth printing below 5% in the third quarter; gross margin falling more than the guided seasonal amount; the fiscal-2027 guide sacrificing the 100-basis-point margin algorithm to fund reinvestment - which the chief financial officer has explicitly left open, saying 'we have not yet determined the appropriate levels of reinvestment for 2027'; or any sign that clinic integration is consuming more capital than advertised.
consensus_delta:
Wall Street is wrong on this name in both directions at once, which is unusual and is the reason it is interesting without being compelling.

Where the street is too bullish. The consensus target is $29.64 with a median of $29.00 and Morgan Stanley at $36.00 as of 10 September 2026 - between 41% and 75% above the current $20.61 and comfortably above my own $24.00 base case. Those targets are built on a free-cash-flow figure that is not free cash flow to owners. The company will generate roughly $730 million this year on management's guided 80% conversion of about $912 million of adjusted operating cash profit, which on an $8.5 billion market value is an 8.6% yield and looks like an obvious bargain after a 49% fall. But roughly $320 million a year of that is share-based compensation added back as non-cash, and the company must spend comparable real cash on buybacks simply to keep the share count from rising - $453 million in the first half alone. The honest owner yield is nearer 4%-5%. Equivalently: reported earnings are about $0.78 a share this year and consensus is roughly $1.06 for the year to January 2028, so the stock is on 26 times this year and 19 times next. Nobody carrying a $30-plus target is underwriting a 19-times multiple on 6% revenue growth; they are underwriting a cash yield that does not exist net of dilution.

Where the street is too bearish. The 9 September reaction - an 11% fall, followed by downgrades from Evercore ISI on 10 September and JPMorgan on 11 September - was triggered by a quarterly free-cash-flow print of $90 million against $106 million, in a quarter where sales came in at the high end of guidance, operating cash profit margin beat, and both the sales range and the low end of the margin range were raised. Management called the cash-flow dip 'entirely timing related' and reaffirmed 80% full-year conversion; on a trailing-twelve-month basis free cash flow is $568 million against $463 million a year earlier, up 23%. Downgrading a franchise on one quarter of working-capital timing, in the same week the ten-year Treasury closed above 5% for the first time since 2007, is macro repricing dressed as fundamental analysis.

Where nobody is looking at all. Two things. First, reported growth of 7.3% is being read as the growth rate; organic growth is 5.7% and decelerating from 8.3% a year ago, with the gap bought for roughly $575 million of acquisitions in six months. Second, and larger: across six earnings calls not one analyst question interrogates the return on capital of buying 29 veterinary clinics, the labour economics of employing veterinarians in a national shortage, or why a company with a negative cash conversion cycle took an inaugural $600 million term loan to do it. Management concedes Modern Animal is dilutive to margin. No published model carries a case in which the clinic roll-up earns less than its cost of capital - and the industry's history of exactly that outcome is long.

The net of it: the market's $29 is too high, the market's panic is too low, and the business is worth roughly $24. That is a real disagreement with consensus, but it is not a large enough disagreement with the price to constitute an edge today.
forcing_function:
There is no binding dated event here - no deal, no proxy contest, no court date, no regulatory decision. This is a re-rating that has to be earned quarter by quarter, and a director should size it accordingly rather than wait for a trigger that does not exist.

The nearest genuine checkpoints, in order:

1. Third-quarter results, expected early-to-mid December 2026 (the prior year's report was 10 December 2025; Chewy had not announced the 2026 date as of 22 September). The specific tests: does organic growth hold the guided 5.3%-6.2%, and does gross margin fall only by the guided seasonal amount once the roughly $15 million of one-off benefits reverse. A clean print against a deliberately lowered bar is the single most likely trigger for the multiple to recover, precisely because management has pre-warned the market to expect a softer quarter.

2. The fiscal-2027 guidance at the fourth-quarter call, around March 2027. This is the real forcing event. It is where the roughly $50 million of annualised artificial-intelligence savings either shows up in the margin algorithm or is spent on reinvestment, and where the path toward the 10% long-term margin target is either reaffirmed with numbers or quietly stretched. The chief financial officer has explicitly reserved that decision.

3. The first disclosed contribution from Modern Animal. Management has kept the acquisition's roughly 100,000 customers out of guidance and promised to break them out separately when integration allows, as they did with SmartPak's 43,000. That disclosure is the first look at whether a $400 million clinic purchase is earning its cost of capital - the single unexamined item in the whole thesis.

4. The buyback, continuously. At $453 million a half against a $8.5 billion market value, the company is retiring roughly 5% of itself a year at these prices. Each quarter the stock stays here, per-share value compounds faster than the business does.

5. Any further registered sale by the controlling private-equity holder would be the opposite - the event that caps the stock rather than releases it - but it would also, once completed, remove the overhang permanently.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are set up badly on the visible lines, and management has pre-announced most of it.

Third-quarter results, expected early-to-mid December 2026 (last year's report was 10 December; the date was not yet announced as of 22 September). Management has already guided gross margin to fall sequentially as the one-off benefits reverse - roughly $10 million of tariff refunds that arrived early, rebates pulled forward out of the second half, and over $5 million of gift-card breakage, inventory adjustments and vendor funds, which together they said 'accounted for essentially all' of the second-quarter profit beat. On top of that, advertising and marketing spend rises in the second half and is weighted to the third quarter, and fuel is a mid-single-digit-million headwind. Guided operating cash profit margin for the quarter is 6.6%-6.7%, below the 6.8% just printed. A market that sold an 11% hole in the stock on a timing-related cash-flow dip will have a genuinely softer optical quarter to work with.

The holiday quarter, reported around March 2027, is where the consumer risk actually sits. The weakness in this business is precisely discretionary attachment - treats slowed materially faster than core food, and hard goods and gifting are the fourth quarter's swing factors. Management will not size treats when asked.

The fiscal-2027 guide, given at that same March 2027 call, is the real event. The chief financial officer has explicitly left the reinvestment question open: 'we have not yet determined the appropriate levels of reinvestment for 2027'. With organic growth at 5.7% and a redesigned membership programme, a refreshed brand campaign and clinic integration all competing for money, there is a live possibility the 100-basis-point margin algorithm is traded away to defend growth. That would remove the one claim that has been reliably true for three years.

There is no financing cliff. Net debt is $549 million including capitalised leases and roughly $22 million excluding them, against about $730 million of annual free cash flow and over $1 billion of available liquidity. But the inaugural $600 million term loan will carry meaningful interest at today's rates - net interest expense is guided at only $10-15 million this year because it is a part-year, and it steps up next year.

Macro is the largest near-term risk and it is not in the company's control. The current regime is a synchronised global tightening: the Federal Reserve raised on 16 September 2026 with 16 of 18 policymakers pointing to another, the ten-year Treasury printed its first close at or above 5% since 2007, Brent is near $100, core producer prices are running 4.7% and consumer sentiment is 47.8. Notably, this thesis does not require a rate cut to work - management's own guidance assumes no consumer recovery at all, which is a structural point in its favour under a regime that punishes rate-rescue theses. But a 19-times-forward consumer name whose marginal holder was a growth fund is exactly the duration being repriced, and the multiple can compress further regardless of the operating result. One housekeeping note: the tariff refunds that helped the quarter are a one-off recovery tied to unresolved trade litigation, not a run-rate benefit.
positioning_washout:
There is no dividend and no yield-focused shareholder base, so the mechanical seller is not an income fund - it is the growth mandate and the sponsor.

The sponsor overhang is the cleanest non-fundamental supply in the name: zero open-market insider purchases against 26 open-market sales totalling roughly 41.2 million shares. The scale of that - far beyond what executive disposals would produce - is consistent with the continuing sell-down of the private-equity position that has controlled Chewy since the PetSmart era. That supply arrives on strength and caps rallies, and it is the reason the buy-side treats every bounce as an exit rather than an entry.

The growth-mandate liquidation is visible in the tape. The stock is 49% below its $40.55 high of the past year, down about 34% year to date, sitting 18% below its 200-day average of $25.19 and 8% below its 50-day average of $22.40, and only 13% up from the bottom of its 52-week range. It made a low of $17.40. A name that compounds sales at 6% and reported earnings at 19 times no longer screens as a growth compounder, and the funds that owned it for the compounding story have been forced out by their own screens rather than by any view on the business.

The signature capitulation event has already occurred: on 9 September 2026 the shares fell about 11% intraday on a quarter that beat on sales and profit and raised full-year guidance. Selling into a raised guide is the behaviour of a shareholder base capitulating on the multiple, not on the fundamentals. But the wash-out is not complete - the $17.40 low has not been retested, and the two downgrades that followed (Evercore ISI on 10 September, JPMorgan to Neutral with a $24 target on 11 September) came after the fall, not before it, which typically means there is still rating-driven selling to come. Fifteen of the twenty most recent broker actions remain at buy-equivalent, so the downgrade cycle is early, not late.

The one large offsetting buyer is the company. Chewy repurchased 9.9 million shares for $200 million in the latest quarter and $453 million in the first half, cutting the diluted count about 2% sequentially, and stated it considers the shares undervalued. That is a real, price-insensitive bid underneath the stock, and it is the reason a full flush to the high teens may be brief if it comes.
moderator_conclusion:
Chewy is a good business at a price the corrected arithmetic makes more interesting than my first pass concluded - and still not, in this tape, a cheap one.

What is genuinely true about the business is unchanged. This is the best operator in American pet retail, and the numbers say so rather than the narrative. Adjusted operating cash profit margin has gone from 4.8% to a guided 6.7%-6.8% in two years against a 10% long-term target, and it has done so while the category was flat - which is exactly what management said would happen when it claimed in March 2026 that 'our model does not depend on a minimum net sales growth threshold to expand profitability'. Autoship subscription revenue is 84.6% of sales and growing faster than the company. Active customers reached 21.7 million with every part of the funnel improving. Return on invested capital of roughly 12.9% is four times Petco's. The cash conversion cycle is negative. The share count is shrinking - 17.5 million shares retired for $400.0 million in the first half. And the credibility record is good: management disclosed, unprompted, that every dollar of its own profit beat last quarter was timing and one-off items, which is not the behaviour of a team managing to a quarter.

What has changed is the bridge, and it changes the decision rather than the thesis. My first pass deducted $549 million of net debt including what it called capitalised leases. Chewy has no material finance lease: the $527.2 million is the non-current operating lease liability, rent is expensed within selling and administrative costs at $30.3 million in the quarter and $57.6 million in the half, so adjusted operating cash profit is already struck after it - and the Petco and Central Garden multiples my segments are benchmarked against are set on the same after-rent convention - while the $42.3 million current lease liability had additionally been counted inside borrowings. The filing's own bridge is debt of $591.7 million less $612.2 million of cash and marketable securities: net cash of $20.5 million. Applied to my unchanged enterprise values, that adds $1.29 a share at every level - adverse $17.34, base $25.26, favourable $33.19. Against $20.61 the central arithmetic inverts: roughly 23% of upside to the base case against roughly 16% of downside to the adverse case, a reward to risk of 1.43 where the first pass had 0.74 and concluded, on that basis, that the reward did not pay for the risk. That conclusion does not survive its own correction, and I withdraw it.

What survives is that the cheapness is smaller than the headline. An 8.6% free-cash-flow yield becomes 4%-5% once you deduct the roughly $320 million a year of stock compensation the company adds back and then spends real cash to neutralise. And the $0.78 of reported earnings this year is itself flattered by about six cents - $24.0 million of non-recurring net legal settlement proceeds sitting in other income, below the operating cash profit line - so the multiple on honest earnings is closer to 29 times this year than the 26 times the reported figure implies. The discount to my corrected $25.26 is 18.4%, which misses the 20% entry bar this book requires in the current environment. It misses by under two points: the bar clears at about $20.21, some 2% below today, not at the $18.00 I originally named. That $18.00 is 29% off the corrected fair value and under 4% above the corrected adverse case, which is a deeper demand than this book's own rule, and I am not going to defend it now that the arithmetic behind it has been withdrawn.

On the catalyst I apply the neutrality rule unchanged. The load-bearing driver is undated and non-binding - an artificial-intelligence savings programme, a buyback, two integrations - and the most recent dated event, the 9 September results, has already fired and went against the stock. Neither fact moves my conviction up or down.

The grade, re-checked against the corrected numbers rather than re-argued. Verdict B, conviction 3 and the underwrite tier stand, and they now stand for a better reason than they did. A reward to risk of 1.43 with no dated forcing function, a narrow moat and a flat category with no pricing is what a 3 is for in this book; it is not the closer-to-three-to-one asymmetry with a trigger on the calendar that takes a name to 4. Two further facts adopted from the skeptic cut the other way and roughly offset the balance-sheet improvement: the six cents of legal settlement inside reported earnings, and the automatic shelf filed on 14 September 2026, five days after the print and near the lows, refreshing the sponsor resale channel this record already names as the thing that caps rallies. What the correction genuinely repairs is the reasoning. A 3 resting on 'the reward does not pay for the risk' was a grade held up by business quality against its own arithmetic; a 3 resting on 1.43 to 1, an 18.4% discount and no trigger is the same number honestly earned.

One risk I want left on the record, restated on the corrected facts. Chewy is not the company it was eighteen months ago. In December 2025 it described itself as debt-free; on 23 June 2026 it drew an inaugural $600 million seven-year term loan at SOFR plus 175 basis points, and it has spent $552.8 million of cash on an equine supplements business it says needs fixing and 29 physical veterinary clinics it concedes dilute margin. The leverage objection is gone - the company is in a small net cash position - but the capital-allocation objection is not, and it is sharper for being unlevered: across six earnings calls not one analyst asked what return that capital will earn. Veterinary roll-ups are capital-hungry, constrained by a national shortage of veterinarians, and have a long record of being overpaid for. If that pivot disappoints, it will not show up in the sales line - it will show up as capital that never came back.

The call: still wait, but the wait is now short and the trigger is priced honestly. Buy when the discount clears this book's 20% bar, which happens at about $20.21 - roughly 2% below today - or on a clean third-quarter print in December that shows organic growth holding above 5% and gross margin falling only by the guided seasonal amount, a bar management has deliberately set low. Either turns this from a fair price into a real one. Until then it is a watchlist name with a good business inside it, a balance sheet that is quietly in net cash, and a company retiring its own stock while we wait.

peer_comps_note:
The supplied peer file reads Chewy as expensive against its peers, on the basis that 15.5 times free cash flow looks rich beside Petco. Tested against live multiples on 22 September 2026, that verdict is only half right, and the half that is wrong matters.

Live enterprise multiples: Chewy - enterprise value $9.06 billion, 0.70 times sales, about 9.9 times this year's guided adjusted operating cash profit (about 15 times after deducting stock compensation), 2.2 times gross profit, return on invested capital about 12.9%. Petco (WOOF) - enterprise value $1.88 billion, 0.31 times sales, 5.55 times operating cash profit, net debt 3.49 times operating cash profit, return on capital 3.3%. Central Garden & Pet (CENT) - enterprise value $2.92 billion, 0.95 times sales, 7.46 times operating cash profit, 3.1 times gross profit, return on capital 5.8%. Amazon - 3.77 times sales, 11.5 times operating cash profit, return on capital 8.5%. BARK is sub-scale and unprofitable and yields no usable multiple.

So Chewy trades at a large premium to Petco, a premium to Central Garden on operating cash profit but a discount to it on gross profit (2.2 times against 3.1 times), and a discount to Amazon - while earning roughly four times Petco's return on capital and carrying essentially no net debt excluding leases against Petco's 3.5 times leverage. Petco's 5.5 times is a distress-and-leverage multiple on a shrinking store base, not a fair anchor for a share-gaining online franchise, and the free-cash-flow comparison the peer file leans on is distorted by Petco's tiny $697 million equity stub sitting beneath $1.18 billion of net debt.

One honest caveat against crediting the whole gap as company-specific edge: Chewy and Petco are driven by the same unresolved variable - a flat American pet category with no pricing and no household-formation growth. That shared driver is sector beta, and a large part of both stocks' de-rating this year is the same trade. What is genuinely company-specific is the quality gap: 12.9% against 3.3% returns on capital, an unlevered balance sheet against a levered one, and growth at two to three times the category against share loss. My read is that Chewy is fairly priced rather than rich - the fall from $40.55 to $20.61 has already done the work the peer file's verdict anticipated.

# Chewy, Inc. (CHWY) — Forensic Interrogator Dossier
**Prepared 2026-09-22 · share price used: $20.605 (NYSE, US dollars, live quote 2026-09-22) · market value about $8.5 billion**
**Transcripts reviewed:** Q4 FY2024 (2025-03-26), Q1 FY2025 (2025-06-11), Q2 FY2025 (2025-09-10), Q3 FY2025 (2025-12-10), Q4/full-year FY2025 (2026-03-25), plus the Q2 FY2026 call (2026-09-09) pulled live because the supplied transcript bundle stops in March 2026 and the two most decision-relevant quarters of the company's history happened after it.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across six calls the story moves through three distinct chapters, and the break between the second and third is the whole investment question.

**Chapter one — "the inflection" (March 2025 to December 2025).** The pitch is a recovery story with a widening profit engine. Chewy had just posted its first year of customer growth in eight quarters (20.5 million active customers, up 2.1%), and chief executive Sumit Singh framed it as structural: *"we believe that we have reached an inflection point with respect to active customer growth"* (Q4 FY2024). Every call that year layered a new profit driver onto the same base: sponsored advertising (a retail-media business selling ad space on Chewy's own site) reaching roughly 1% of sales with a stated ceiling of 3%; the Chewy Vet Care clinic network going from 8 to 18 locations; the Chewy Plus paid membership launching at $49 and repriced to $79 within nine months; the Get Real fresh-food private brand; and the SmartPak equine acquisition announced 30 October 2025. Profitability compounded as advertised — adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (a rough proxy for operating cash profit, "adjusted EBITDA") margin went 4.8% in FY2024 to 5.8% in Q3 FY2025, and the company finished Q3 FY2025 *"debt-free"* with about $675 million of cash.

**Chapter two — "the algorithm doesn't need the market" (March 2026).** At the FY2025 year-end call management made an unusually specific promise. Singh opened not with results but with a macro stance: *"We expect 2026 pet industry dynamics to largely mirror 2025, steady and resilient to macro trends, but without cyclical acceleration. Pet household formation appears stable with no evidence of deterioration."* He then de-linked profit from demand outright: *"our model does not depend on a minimum net sales growth threshold to expand profitability."* Artificial intelligence was introduced as a new margin lever with a hard number attached — low tens of millions of dollars of savings in 2026, about $50 million annualised in 2027. The message was that the compounding was self-generated and macro-proof.

**Chapter three — "we reset" (June 2026 to today).** That framing lasted roughly five weeks. On the Q2 FY2026 call Singh said it plainly: *"The stability that we were expecting coming into Q1 started deteriorating a bit in the late March, April time frame, which is what you heard us comment on our Q1 earnings call, and we reset our guidance at that particular point."* Organic growth — growth excluding acquisitions — decelerated to 5.7% in Q2 FY2026 from 8.3% a year earlier. The language flipped from offence to preservation: *"we are not assuming a meaningful consumer recovery for the balance of this fiscal year… our confidence remains grounded in what we can control."*

The quieter and larger shift is in what the company **is**. In December 2025 Chewy described itself as debt-free and asset-light. By August 2026 it had spent roughly $575 million on two acquisitions in six months — SmartPak (about $175 million, equine health) and Modern Animal (about $400 million, 29 owned veterinary clinics with round-the-clock virtual care) — and funded them with a $600 million *"inaugural term loan."* An online retailer with negative working capital has, inside two quarters, become a leveraged owner of physical veterinary real estate and licensed clinical labour. Nothing in the narrative arc was dropped; a genuinely different balance sheet was added underneath it.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining — from expansive to defensive, with the pivot dated precisely to April 2026.**

- **Q4 FY2024 (March 2025) — peak offence.** *"The durability and power of our highly predictable business model shined."* *"We are increasingly confident in our ability to reach our long-term adjusted EBITDA margin target of 10%."*
- **Q1 FY2025 (June 2025) — confident, still growth-first.** *"The momentum at Chewy continues."* Specific, checkable forecasts: about $550 million of free cash flow for the year.
- **Q2 FY2025 (September 2025) — expansive.** New products (Get Real), new capacity *"through 2028,"* a membership programme showing *"strong product market fit."*
- **Q3 FY2025 (December 2025) — confident and concrete.** *"Profits once again growing faster than sales."* Capital expenditure guided **below** the low end of the range. Debt-free, $1.5 billion of liquidity.
- **Q4 FY2025 (March 2026) — the over-reach.** The most emphatic macro call in the file (*"steady and resilient to macro trends"*) is made in the same breath as the most emphatic profit promise. This is the only place in six calls where management forecasts the external world rather than its own execution, and it is the only place they are proved wrong.
- **Q2 FY2026 (September 2026) — defensive.** The vocabulary is now containment: *"we did not see a meaningful recovery… Importantly, however, we did not see further deterioration."* *"The things we can control."* Growth language is replaced by cost language — AI savings, variable cost to serve, fulfilment utilisation, *"disciplined headcount management."* The one forward-looking growth item offered is a *"refreshed program design"* for the membership that Singh could only describe with a joke about bad marketing copy.

Guidance has become *more* specific over time, not less — quarterly sales, quarterly margin, quarterly earnings per share, a share count, a tax rate, a capital-expenditure ratio. That is the behaviour of a team confident in its own model even while it is nervous about the weather.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High on what they control. Low on macro forecasting — which they have now stopped doing.**

| FY2024 sales and margin (given March 2025) | Exceeded the high end of both; adjusted EBITDA margin 4.8%, the top of the range |
| "Active customer growth in 2025" (March 2025) | Delivered every quarter: 20.5m to 20.8m to 20.9m to 21.2m to 21.7m |
| "Approximately $550 million of free cash flow" in FY2025 (June 2025) | Beat it — FY2025 free cash flow was roughly $600 million+ |
| FY2025 capital expenditure of 1.5%-2% of sales (March 2025) | Came in at 1.3%, below the low end — spent less, not more |

| Q1-Q3 FY2025 quarterly sales | Above the high end of the range, three quarters running |

| **FY2026 outlook as framed in March 2026** | **Cut in June 2026, then partially restored in September 2026** |

The beat rate in the screener data (5 of 7 quarters, 71%) understates the operating record and overstates the certainty. There is mild sandbagging in the sales ranges — management has hit the high end so often that the midpoint is effectively the floor — but there is no sandbagging in the margin guide, which is set tight (6.7%-6.8%) and defended with mechanics.

The material debit is a single, dated, self-inflicted one: on 25 March 2026 management told the market the pet category was *"steady and resilient to macro trends"* and by 10 June 2026 they had reset guidance because the category deteriorated in late March and April. They owned it on the record. But a director should take the lesson: **Chewy forecasts Chewy well and forecasts the American pet owner badly.** Underwrite the first and ignore the second.

**Score: High on execution, Medium overall.**

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **The one question they will not answer: how much of consumables is treats.** Steven Forbes of Guggenheim asked directly in Q2 FY2026. Singh: *"I will stay away from precisely defining the penetration of treats within the business,"* followed by four hundred words about jerky, dental and freeze-dried varieties. Treats are the piece that *"slowed more sharply than growth in core food" —* it is the cleanest read on consumer stress in the business, and they will not size it.
- **Reinvestment versus margin — unresolved and now urgent.** Nathaniel Feather of Morgan Stanley asked whether Chewy would spend to reaccelerate growth. The chief financial officer's answer: *"we have not yet determined the appropriate levels of reinvestment for 2027."* With organic growth at 5.7% and a hundred-basis-point margin promise, something has to give in the FY2027 guide, and management has explicitly reserved the right to decide later.
- **Modern Animal's contribution is excluded from guidance.** Singh: the acquired platform has *"roughly 100 thousand customers"* of which *"40 to 50"* percent are new to Chewy, but *"presently, when we are giving you forecasting, it is not including the Modern Animal net adds."* That is prudent, and it also means the reported customer-growth number is about to get a mechanical boost that has nothing to do with the funnel. Watch for it to be presented as momentum.
- **The pressure point that already turned into bad news.** Through 2025 analysts repeatedly probed household formation and whether the category would normalise. Management kept saying they were not underwriting a rebound — while simultaneously describing the category as stable. It was not stable, and the stock has halved.
- **What nobody is pushing on, and should be.** In six calls, not one analyst question in the transcripts interrogates the returns on capital of buying veterinary clinics, the labour economics of employing veterinarians, or why a company with negative working capital took on a $600 million term loan to do it. The clinic roll-up is being graded entirely on management's own satisfaction scores.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**🔴 Red flags**

- **The macro call broke in five weeks.** "Steady and resilient" (25 March 2026) to a guidance reset (10 June 2026).
- **A balance-sheet identity change, quietly executed.** *"Remain debt-free"* (Q3 FY2025) to a $600 million inaugural term loan and $1.16 billion of total debt (Q2 FY2026). Net debt of $549 million including capitalised leases; roughly zero excluding them. This is not yet dangerous — it is about half a year of cash profit — but it removes the fortress framing.
- **Growth is being bought at the margin.** Reported 7.3%, organic 5.7%. About $575 million spent on acquisitions in six months against roughly $730 million of expected annual free cash flow.
- **Three people in the finance chair in fifteen months.** David Reeder departed June 2025 for a semiconductor chief-executive role; Will Billings served as interim; Chris Deppe was appointed 24 February 2026. The head of investor relations also changed between the March and September 2026 calls.
- **Insider behaviour is one-directional.** Zero open-market purchases against 26 sales totalling roughly 41.2 million shares. The bulk is a sponsor selling down rather than executives fleeing, but the direction of travel is unambiguous and the supply is real.
- **Reported free cash flow is flattered by about $320 million a year of stock compensation** that the company then spends real cash to neutralise.
- **The Q2 beat was mechanical.** Roughly $15 million of tariff-refund timing, pulled-forward rebates, gift-card breakage and vendor funds — *"essentially all"* of the outperformance by management's own account.

**🟢 Green flags**

- **The margin promise is being kept, quarter after quarter.** 4.8% (FY2024) to 5.6% (FY2025) to 6.7%-6.8% guided (FY2026), against a 10% long-term target. That is over 200 basis points delivered in two years while the category was flat.
- **Management pre-empted its own low-quality beat.** Disclosing that every dollar of upside was timing, before a single analyst asked, is the behaviour of a team that expects to be here in five years.
- **The recurring base keeps thickening.** Autoship subscription sales were 79.2% of revenue in FY2024 and 84.6% in Q2 FY2026, and they grew 9.3% against total growth of 7.3%. Customers went 20.5 million to 21.7 million across six quarters, and net additions never stopped.
- **Capital expenditure came in *below* guidance** in FY2025 (1.3% against a 1.5%-2.0% range) while capacity was built through 2028. Fulfilment capacity is pre-funded.
- **Genuine per-share shrinkage.** Diluted shares fell from 428.4 million (Q2 FY2025) to 410.1 million (Q2 FY2026), about 4%, and management is buying because *"we continue to believe that Chewy shares are undervalued at current levels."*
- **Negative cash conversion cycle of about three days.** Customers pay before suppliers do; growth funds itself.
- **Return on invested capital of roughly 12.9%** against 3.3% at Petco and 5.8% at Central Garden & Pet — by a distance the best operator in its comparison set.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **"Structural" became the tell-word.** From Q3 FY2025 onward, margin gains are described as *"structural"* — *"structurally enhance our margins,"* *"structurally lowering our cost to serve,"* *"structural wallet share gains."* The word is doing the job the growth rate used to do.
- **Retail media is being pre-managed downward.** In FY2024 sponsored advertising was *"the largest contributor to year-over-year gross margin improvement."* By March 2026 the chief financial officer says the impact will *"taper a bit in 2026"* and Singh reframes it as a mix effect, not a growth issue: revenue shifting to lower-margin off-site advertising. The highest-multiple piece of Chewy is flattening at roughly half its stated 3%-of-sales ceiling.
- **The membership programme is being rebuilt, not scaled.** Chewy Plus went from *"strong product market fit"* (Q2 FY2025) to a price rise from $49 to $79 (October 2025) to *"a refreshed program design"* needed to *"deliver that compelling product market fit that I have been talking about"* (Q2 FY2026). That is the third repositioning in eighteen months. The Prime and Costco analogies have quietly disappeared.
- **Management named its own terminal risk out loud.** Singh, March 2026: *"we are closely following the emergence of Agentic Commerce models and view it as a future incremental demand and distribution channel."* An artificial-intelligence shopping agent that buys the dog food is a threat to the interface habit that underpins Autoship, and he framed it as an opportunity. Watch the framing, not the claim.
- **The new chief financial officer sounds different.** Deppe's first full quarter is materially more forensic than his predecessors — itemising $10 million of timing, over $5 million of discrete items, naming a fuel headwind, and pre-announcing that gross margin will fall sequentially in Q3. Reeder and Billings sold the story; Deppe is showing the workings. For an investor that is an upgrade.
- **An acquired-customer count is about to flatter the funnel.** SmartPak added 43,000 customers to Q2's active count. Modern Animal's roughly 100,000 will land in Q3 or Q4. On a base adding roughly 208,000 organically per quarter, that is a meaningful optical boost that management has so far promised to separate.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The earnings engine is stable and improving; the capital allocation has changed character. In nine months Chewy went from a debt-free, asset-light retailer returning all surplus cash to shareholders, to a company carrying $1.16 billion of gross debt that has spent $575 million buying an equine supplements business it says *"requires a little bit of fixing"* and 29 veterinary clinics. Both may prove excellent. Neither is the business the market has been underwriting since 2019.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *the true owner-earnings yield, not the headline free-cash-flow yield.* Chewy will generate roughly $730 million of reported free cash flow this year on an $8.5 billion market value — an 8.6% yield that makes the stock look obviously cheap after a 49% fall from its high. But roughly $320 million of that is share-based compensation added back, and the company must spend comparable real cash on buybacks simply to hold the share count still. On the honest measure the yield is closer to 4%-5%. That is a fair price for a 6%-growth franchise with expanding margins — it is not a bargain, and the gap between the two numbers is precisely the gap between the $29-$36 price targets on the street and where this business is actually worth owning.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and widening.** The moat type is **switching costs layered on scale-cost advantage**, with a genuine intangible-brand overlay. Autoship at 84.6% of sales is habit and convenience made into contracted repeat revenue; the negative cash conversion cycle and pre-built automated fulfilment give a real unit-cost edge; the licensed pharmacy, compounding operation (management notes only two credible compounders exist nationally) and now the owned clinics are the parts a competitor genuinely cannot copy quickly. The evidence says **widening, not eroding**: gross margin up from 29.8% to 30.4%, adjusted EBITDA margin up over 200 basis points in two years, return on invested capital roughly 12.9% and rising, and market share gains at two to three times category growth in a flat market. It is narrow rather than wide for one reason — Amazon sells identical bags of the same food at scale, the category has no pricing power by management's own admission (*"little or no contribution from pricing"*), and the differentiation is service and habit rather than a product a rival cannot obtain.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The structural force to watch is agentic commerce — artificial-intelligence shopping agents that buy on the customer's behalf and, in doing so, strip out the interface loyalty that makes Autoship sticky and push the contest back to price, where Amazon wins. It is real and management has named it. It is not terminal, for three reasons: pet food is an emotional, trust-led, repeat purchase where Chewy's brand is measurably strong; roughly 30% of revenue now runs through pharmacy, compounding, insurance and clinics, which are licensed or physical and cannot be disintermediated by a shopping agent; and the category itself is growing and shifting online, with Chewy the beneficiary of that shift rather than its victim. The cheapness here is a **fear-print on a de-rating multiple, not a structurally shrinking base** — but it is a modest fear-print, not a deep one, and a director should size it accordingly.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend widening · structural threat manageable.

moderator_conclusion: Wait for the wash-out, conviction 3 of 5, unchanged from the prior look. Sources: six quarterly earnings calls from March 2025 through September 9, 2026 (the September 2026 call pulled live from FMP because the bundled transcript file stops at March 2026), the screener's financial trajectory, FMP trailing-twelve-month (TTM) cash-flow data to 2026-08-02, and dated news flow through 2026-09-25.*

**Bottom line:** Chewy is the best-run pure-play pet retailer in the United States, and the numbers largely corroborate what management says about share gains, recurring revenue and margin expansion. What has changed in 2026 is the backdrop, not the operator: the pet consumer has weakened (treats, toppers and premium food are being traded down), management reset its outlook in June, and the September quarter's profit beat was, by the company's own admission, almost entirely one-off items. The balance sheet has also changed character — Chewy went from debt-free to carrying a $600 million term loan to buy Modern Animal and fund a large buyback. Credibility is good, not flawless.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **March 2025 (Q4 fiscal 2024):** a victory-lap tone. Active customers returned to growth "for the first time in eight quarters," adjusted EBITDA margin (operating cash profit before stock pay, as a share of sales) reached 4.8%, and management said it was "increasingly confident" in a 10% long-term margin target. Growth drivers were Autoship (the free repeat-delivery subscription), sponsored ads (then about 1% of sales, "up to 3%" long-term), and Chewy Vet Care clinics.
- **June to December 2025 (Q1 to Q3 fiscal 2025):** the story broadened. Chewy+ (a paid membership) came out of beta in June 2025, the Get Real fresh-food private brand launched in August 2025, the SmartPak equine acquisition was announced October 30, 2025, and the Chewy+ fee was raised from $49 to $79 at the end of October 2025. Sales beat the top of guidance every quarter. The CFO, David Reeder, left in June 2025; an interim finance chief ran two calls.
- **March 2026 (Q4 fiscal 2025):** the first defensive framing appears. The CEO opened with an industry essay instead of results, said the company was "not underwriting a meaningful rebound" in pet household formation, and pre-emptively argued that "our model does not depend on a minimum net sales growth threshold to expand profitability." AI savings (low tens of millions in 2026, about $50 million a year by 2027) entered the story as a new margin lever. Chris Deppe was named permanent CFO.
- **June 2026 (Q1 fiscal 2026):** by management's own later description, the outlook was "reset ... to reflect a more cautious consumer environment."
- **September 9, 2026 (Q2 fiscal 2026):** "stabilized" is the key word — no recovery, "no further deterioration." Organic sales growth slowed to 5.7%; the Modern Animal veterinary chain was bought for $400 million, a $600 million inaugural term loan was raised, and $200 million of stock was repurchased in the quarter. The growth pitch has migrated from "e-commerce share gains" toward "Chewy Health" (clinics, pharmacy, compounding, equine) plus AI productivity.

The arc is expansion-then-consolidation: the core retail engine is now pitched as a steady share-gainer in a flat market, with health and acquisitions carrying the growth narrative.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Stable, with a defensive tilt since March 2026.**

- March 2025: offensive — "an extraordinary year," "increasingly confident" on 10%.
- June to December 2025: offensive and specific — hard numbers on Chewy+ (3% of July 2025 sales), clinic counts, capex below range.
- March 2026: shift to pre-emptive defense — "not underwriting a meaningful rebound," "does not depend on a minimum net sales growth threshold."
- September 2026: measured — "did not see a meaningful recovery ... did not see further deterioration"; unusual candor about one-offs. The CEO declined to size treats as a share of consumables. A widely quoted line from that call: "dog seems to be worsening; cat seems to be strengthening."

Specificity has held up; the language has moved from growth to control ("what we can control," "does not depend on a meaningful recovery").

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

- FY24: sales beat the top of the range; adjusted EBITDA margin hit the upper end (4.8%).
- FY25: sales above the high end in each of Q1, Q2 and Q3; guidance raised in Q2 2025 by $175M at the midpoint; clinic openings (10) hit the high end of 8-10.
- FY26: the June 2026 reset lowered expectations; September 2026 narrowed organic growth to 5.5%-6.3% and lifted the low end of margin guidance by 0.1 point.
- The screener's beat rate is 5 of 7 quarters (71%).

**Reliability: High on sales and margin delivery; Medium on the macro read** — management was too confident on the consumer in March 2026 and had to reset in June. There is a mild sandbagging pattern on sales (consistently landing at the top of ranges).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Discretionary pressure:** analysts repeatedly probe treats, premium food and hard goods; management deflects on sizing.
- **Chewy+ economics:** pushed for targets since 2025; management "will stay away from providing immediate targets."
- **Acquisition integration:** Modern Animal's customer additions and conversion to Autoship have not been sized; the business is a modest margin drag.
- **Free cash flow quality:** the September 2026 cash miss was the proximate cause of the 11% one-day fall on 2026-09-09; two downgrades followed within two sessions (JPMorgan cut to a neutral-equivalent with a $24 target on 2026-09-11).
- **Unaddressed:** the size of stock-based pay relative to cash profit, and why buybacks are now levered.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- 🔴 September 2026 profit beat was essentially all timing and one-off items (CFO, Q2 fiscal 2026).
- 🔴 Balance sheet turned from debt-free with $675M cash (December 2025) to a $600M term loan (Q2 fiscal 2026); total borrowings $634M plus $527M of capitalized leases against $612M cash.
- 🔴 Stock-based pay of $226M TTM, excluded from every headline profit metric.
- 🔴 Open-market insider and holder selling: 26 sales totalling about 41.2M shares against zero purchases in the screener's window (the seller mix was not verified this run).
- 🔴 Organic growth decelerating: about 8% through 2025 to 5.7% in the September 2026 quarter.
- 🟢 Autoship at a record 84.6% of sales (September 2026), up from about 66% at IPO — revenue is subscription-like.
- 🟢 Active customers 21.7M, up 3.8%, with 208k sequential net additions (September 2026).
- 🟢 Selling, general and administrative leverage of 0.7 point year over year even in a weak market; AI savings are quantified and dated.
- 🟢 Management is buying stock aggressively (9.9M shares in the quarter, about 2% of diluted shares) and says shares are "undervalued at current levels."

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The growth story has quietly shifted from e-commerce share capture ("40 to 50 cents of every dollar moving online," 2025) to "Chewy Health" and acquisitions — a tell that core retail growth has settled in the mid-single digits.
- Sponsored ads: from "the largest contributor" to gross margin (2025) to "we do expect sponsored ads impact to taper a bit" (March 2026) as the mix moves off-site.
- Capital allocation: first acquisitions (SmartPak, Modern Animal) and first debt in the company's public life, within about a year of each other.
- Finance turnover: a CFO departure in June 2025, an interim officer for two quarters, then an internal promotion — continuity, but less outside challenge.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** The operator keeps executing (share gains, customer growth, margin up about a point a year), but top-line growth has slowed and capital allocation has become more aggressive (levered buybacks plus acquisitions).

**The single most important thing to weigh:** what the business earns for owners after stock-based pay. Adjusted EBITDA of about $912M in FY26 turns into roughly $730M of free cash flow and about $500M after stock pay — roughly $1.20 a share. At $18.46 that is about 15 times owner earnings: fair-to-cheap for a durable share-gainer, not a screaming discount.

**Moat:** scale-cost plus a switching-cost element (Autoship habit, pharmacy and vet relationships). Width: narrow. Returns on invested capital are still low (3.9% in the screener) but rising, and margins are expanding rather than falling, so the moat is not eroding. **Secular threat:** manageable — the channel shift to online helps Chewy; the structural risk is Amazon and mass retail pricing, not obsolescence. The cheapness reads as a fear print on a slowing consumer, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

# Chewy (CHWY) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Debate date 2026-10-26. Live price $21.73 (NYSE, USD, FMP quote 2026-10-26). Transcripts covered: five calls, 2025-09-10 (Q2 fiscal 2025) through 2026-09-09 (Q2 fiscal 2026).

**Takeaway.** Chewy is a well-run, share-gaining online pet retailer whose story has stayed remarkably consistent for five quarters: recurring Autoship (automatic repeat ordering) revenue, steady customer additions, and margins that keep expanding. ## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **2025-09-10 (Q2 FY25):** the pitch was operating leverage - sponsored ads, health mix, a new automated fulfilment center, and roughly $125M of buybacks in the quarter.
